s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the magnitude of an earthquake from its intensity?
o: Magnitude denotes observed damage at a place, whereas intensity denotes energy released at the focus
Magnitude varies from place to place, whereas intensity has one value for the entire earthquake
Magnitude denotes energy released at the focus, whereas intensity denotes the observed effects at a particular place
Both magnitude and intensity denote the energy released at the focus
x: Magnitude is the quantitative measure of energy released at the focus and has one value for an earthquake. Intensity is the qualitative measure of observed effects at a particular place and varies with distance from the epicentre.
tq: Split the options by matching each term with its defining measure.
sec: ■ Measurement - magnitude vs intensity, scales and instruments  [APPSC]

s:
With reference to earthquake measurement, consider the following statements:
1. The Richter scale was developed by Charles F. Richter in 1935.
2. The Richter scale is used to measure earthquake intensity.
3. Moment magnitude is based on the rupture area of the fault and the size of seismic waves.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Richter scale measures magnitude, not intensity; intensity is measured using scales such as Modified Mercalli and MSK.
tq: Use the magnitude–intensity distinction to reject the swapped measurement statement.
sec: ■ Measurement - magnitude vs intensity, scales and instruments  [APPSC]

s: An earthquake increases from magnitude 5 to magnitude 6 on the Richter scale. Which one of the following best describes the change?
o: Its wave amplitude becomes 6 times and energy becomes 36 times
Its wave amplitude becomes 31 times and energy released becomes 10 times
Its wave amplitude becomes 10 times and energy released becomes approximately 31 times
Both its wave amplitude and energy released become 10 times
x: An increase of one magnitude unit on the Richter scale represents a tenfold increase in wave amplitude and an approximately 31-fold increase in energy released.
tq: Separate the amplitude factor from the energy factor instead of treating both as identical.
sec: ■ Measurement - magnitude vs intensity, scales and instruments  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements regarding the scales used for earthquake measurement is correct?
o: Modified Mercalli and MSK scales measure magnitude from I to XII
Moment magnitude is a qualitative scale based only on building damage
The Richter scale measures intensity from I to XII
Modified Mercalli and MSK scales measure intensity from I to XII
x: Modified Mercalli and MSK are qualitative intensity scales, each ranging from I to XII. Richter and moment magnitude are magnitude scales.
tq: Discriminate between quantitative magnitude scales and qualitative intensity scales.
sec: ■ Measurement - magnitude vs intensity, scales and instruments  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is the most appropriate reason for the increasing use of the moment magnitude scale for strong earthquakes?
o: It is restricted to shallow crustal earthquakes
It records only the time at which shaking begins
It is based on fault rupture area and seismic-wave size and is suitable for strong earthquakes
It measures only the damage caused to buildings near the epicentre
x: Moment magnitude is based on the rupture area of the fault and the size of seismic waves. It has largely replaced the Richter scale for strong earthquakes.
tq: Identify the instrument or scale by asking what physical quantity it actually measures.
sec: ■ Measurement - magnitude vs intensity, scales and instruments  [APPSC]

s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Instrument)
a. Seismograph
b. Seismometer
c. Seismoscope
d. Tiltmeter

List-II (Function)
i. Sensor used in a seismograph
ii. Shows that a tremor occurred and records its time
iii. Records and measures earthquakes
iv. Measures ground tilt at faults and volcanoes
x: A seismograph records and measures earthquakes; a seismometer is its sensor; a seismoscope only indicates that a tremor occurred and its time; and a tiltmeter measures ground tilt.
tq: Start from the sure instrument–function pair and eliminate codes containing mismatches.
sec: ■ Measurement - magnitude vs intensity, scales and instruments  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the function of a creepmeter?
o: It shows only the time at which a tremor occurred
It measures the tilt of volcanic ground
It measures the slow slip or creep along a fault
It records the energy released at the earthquake focus
x: A creepmeter is used to measure slow slip, or creep, along a fault. Ground tilt is measured by a tiltmeter, while a seismoscope only indicates occurrence and time of a tremor.
tq: Use confusable-instrument discrimination by matching each device with its specific function.
sec: ■ Measurement - magnitude vs intensity, scales and instruments  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements about earthquake prediction is correct?
o: Earthquakes are accurately predicted through the Richter scale
Earthquakes still cannot be predicted accurately
Earthquakes can be predicted accurately only in stable continental regions
Earthquakes can currently be predicted accurately for a precise time and place
x: Despite monitoring and seismological research, earthquakes cannot yet be predicted accurately in terms of their precise time, location and magnitude.
tq: Reject the extreme claim that a measurement scale can provide precise prediction.
sec: ■ Measurement - magnitude vs intensity, scales and instruments  [APPSC]

s: The point inside the Earth where an earthquake rupture begins and energy is released is known as the
x: The focus, also called the hypocentre, is the point of origin of the rupture inside the Earth. The epicentre is the corresponding point on the surface directly above it.
tq: Apply the inside-versus-surface distinction to separate focus from epicentre.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The epicentre is located on the Earth's surface directly above the focus.
2. Shaking is generally strongest at the epicentre.
3. The focus is necessarily located at the Earth's surface.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The focus is an underground point where rupture begins and may be shallow or deep; it is not located at the surface.
tq: Find the false statement by testing the precise location of the focus.

s: Which one of the following depth ranges is typical of ordinary crustal earthquakes?
x: Typical crustal earthquakes begin at depths of about 10–29 km. Earthquakes beginning 80 km or more below the Moho are rare continental mantle earthquakes.
tq: Use the depth-range distinction to separate ordinary crustal events from rare mantle events.

s: Rare continental mantle earthquakes differ from ordinary crustal earthquakes in that they generally begin
o: at the surface above the epicentre
80 km or more below the Moho
x: Rare continental mantle earthquakes originate 80 km or more below the Moho, whereas ordinary crustal earthquakes commonly begin at depths of about 10–29 km.
tq: Compare the two depth categories before selecting the deeper origin.

s:
Arrange the following earthquake-producing settings from the examples given in the correct sequence of boundary type and example:
A. Divergent boundary — Mid-Atlantic Ridge
B. Convergent boundary — Himalaya
C. Transform boundary — San Andreas Fault
D. Volcanic activity — rising magma fracturing rocks
x: The sequence lists the divergent, convergent and transform examples followed by the volcanic mechanism. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Himalaya and San Andreas represent the three major plate-boundary settings.
tq: Match each named example to its process before selecting the sequence.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: The Ring of Fire is associated mainly with volcanic and convergent-margin activity, not with the San Andreas-type transform setting. The San Andreas Fault is the transform-boundary example.
tq: Find the incorrectly assigned boundary type rather than choosing a familiar place name.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s: What is the immediate geological process at a tectonic earthquake source?
o: Stress on a fault exceeds rock strength and the rocks rupture
The weight of ocean water dissolves the crust
The Earth's magnetic field reverses suddenly
Sediments settle in a basin and generate tides
x: A tectonic earthquake occurs when stress accumulated on a fault exceeds the strength of the rocks, causing rupture and the release of seismic waves.
tq: Identify the cause-and-effect chain linking stress, rupture and seismic waves.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s:
Which of the following are examples of intraplate earthquakes associated with hidden faults in relatively stable continental regions?
1. Latur
2. Koyna
3. Jabalpur
4. San Andreas
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Latur, Koyna and Jabalpur are examples of intraplate earthquakes associated with hidden faults in stable regions. San Andreas is a transform plate-boundary fault.
tq: Separate stable-region intraplate examples from a well-known plate-boundary example.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s: The 1993 Latur earthquake is significant in the study of earthquake causes because it demonstrated that
o: earthquakes may occur in stable regions along hidden faults
earthquakes occur only at convergent plate boundaries
all intraplate earthquakes are caused by volcanic eruptions
stable continental regions cannot experience damaging earthquakes
x: The Latur earthquake occurred far from a plate boundary and showed that stable continental regions can experience earthquakes along concealed or old faults.
tq: Use the exception to the plate-boundary rule as the deciding clue.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is regarded as India's classic example of a reservoir-induced earthquake?
x: The Koyna earthquake of 1967 is the classic Indian example of reservoir-induced seismicity, associated with the filling and weight of a large reservoir.
tq: Link the named event and year with the specific earthquake mechanism.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s: Reservoir-induced seismicity is most directly associated with which of the following?
o: The cooling of lava after a volcanic eruption
Only the movement of oceanic plates at mid-ocean ridges
The seasonal expansion of desert sand
Filling of large reservoirs and the weight of stored water
x: The filling of large reservoirs adds water load and can alter stresses and pore pressures in the crust. The Koyna case is the classic example.
tq: Identify the human-induced change that alters crustal stress and pore pressure.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s:
Which of the following activities may also induce earthquakes, usually of low magnitude?
1. Mining
2. Hydraulic fracturing
3. Filling of large reservoirs
4. Movement along the San Andreas Fault
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Mining and hydraulic fracturing are other induced causes, generally producing low-magnitude earthquakes. Reservoir filling is another induced cause, whereas San Andreas movement is tectonic.
tq: Group the human-induced causes and exclude the natural transform-boundary example.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly explains a volcanic earthquake?
o: It results from the conversion of intensity into magnitude
It is caused by rising magma fracturing rocks or the collapse of volcanic structures
It occurs only in stable continental shields far from volcanoes
It results exclusively from the weight of a reservoir
x: Volcanic earthquakes can result when rising magma fractures surrounding rocks or when volcanic structures collapse.
tq: Choose the option containing both parts of the volcanic mechanism.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s: A seismic doublet is best described as
o: two volcanic eruptions separated by a long interval
two independent earthquakes of similar magnitude occurring close together in time and space
a main shock followed by aftershocks that gradually become weaker
two waves arriving at the epicentre at exactly the same time
x: A seismic doublet consists of two independent earthquakes of similar magnitude occurring in quick succession and close together. This differs from an aftershock sequence, which generally tapers off.
tq: Distinguish a doublet from the familiar mainshock–aftershock pattern by focusing on independence and similarity of magnitude.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly relates the Venezuelan seismic doublet to its characteristics?
o: A single magnitude 7.5 earthquake occurred along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
Two reservoir-induced earthquakes occurred at Koyna in 1967
Two earthquakes of magnitudes 7.1 and 7.5 occurred close together on the Caribbean–South American strike-slip boundary
A magnitude 5.1 earthquake was followed by a volcanic eruption in the Himalaya
x: The Venezuelan seismic doublet consisted of earthquakes of magnitude 7.1 and 7.5 in quick succession near the Caribbean–South American strike-slip boundary.
tq: Combine the event’s magnitudes, location and boundary type to identify the complete match.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s: The reported death toll associated with the Venezuelan seismic doublet was
x: The reported toll associated with the Venezuelan seismic doublet was 589 deaths.
tq: Use the exact numerical recall required for a current-affairs-linked geographical event.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s: Seismic seiches are
o: standing waves in rivers, reservoirs and ponds
waves generated only by volcanic ash
x: Seismic seiches are standing waves that may develop in enclosed or partly enclosed water bodies such as rivers, reservoirs and ponds. They were reported during the Myanmar earthquake.
tq: Distinguish a water-body phenomenon from earthquake source types and fault movements.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s: During which event were seismic seiches reported in rivers, reservoirs and ponds?
x: Seismic seiches were reported during the Myanmar earthquake. They are standing waves in water bodies triggered by seismic shaking.
tq: Link the observed secondary phenomenon to the specific earthquake event.
sec: ■ Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic  [APPSC]

s: The Uttarkashi earthquake of 1991, with an approximate magnitude of 6.8, occurred in which setting?
x: The 1991 Uttarkashi earthquake occurred in the Himalayan thrust zone and had an approximate magnitude of 6.8.
tq: Directly identify the earthquake with its tectonic setting.

s: The 1993 Latur earthquake was significant because it occurred in an intraplate region that had earlier been rated as which risk zone?
x: The Latur earthquake occurred in an intraplate region that was then classified as low-risk Zone I.
tq: Use the numerical-zone clue to distinguish a low-risk intraplate event.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: The Bhuj earthquake occurred on 26 January 2001 and had a magnitude of 7.7. The other pairs contain incorrect years or magnitudes.
tq: Start from the sure year–magnitude pair and eliminate swapped entries.

s: The Bhuj earthquake of 2001 led directly to which of the following institutional and legislative developments?
o: The enactment of the Disaster Management Act, 2005 and the establishment of the NDMA
The creation of the Tsunami Early Warning System and GSI
The establishment of the National Centre for Seismology and the RISEQ app
The introduction of Zone VI under IS 1893: 2016
x: The 2001 Bhuj earthquake contributed to the Disaster Management Act, 2005 and the establishment of the National Disaster Management Authority.
tq: Link a major disaster to the institutional response that followed it.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Gorkha earthquake:
1. It occurred in Nepal in 2015.
2. It had a magnitude of 7.8.
3. It occurred along the Main Himalayan Thrust.
4. It caused liquefaction in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All four statements are correct. The 2015 Gorkha earthquake in Nepal had a magnitude of 7.8, occurred along the Main Himalayan Thrust and caused liquefaction in parts of the Gangetic plain.
tq: Verify the event through its year, magnitude, tectonic setting and secondary effect.

s: The 2011 Tohoku earthquake in Japan was associated with which combination?
o: Pacific plate subduction, tsunami and Fukushima
Intraplate movement and the Disaster Management Act, 2005
Himalayan thrust zone and liquefaction in Bihar
x: The 2011 Tohoku earthquake had a magnitude of 9.0, occurred in the Pacific plate subduction setting and was associated with a tsunami and the Fukushima disaster.
tq: Match the earthquake with its distinctive tectonic setting and consequences.

s: The February 2023 earthquake in the Turkey–Syria region occurred along which fault system?
x: The February 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquake, of magnitude 7.8, occurred along the East Anatolian Fault between the Anatolian and Arabian plates.
tq: Discriminate between similarly named regional fault systems.

s: Which of the following correctly describes the 2025 Myanmar earthquake near Mandalay?
o: Magnitude 9.0; Pacific subduction zone; tsunami in Japan
Magnitude 6.2; Himalayan thrust zone; liquefaction in Bihar
Magnitude 7.8; East Anatolian Fault; movement of the Anatolian and Arabian plates
Magnitude 7.7; Sagaing Fault; strike-slip movement involving the Indian and Eurasian plates
x: The 2025 Mandalay earthquake had a magnitude of 7.7 and occurred along the Sagaing Fault, a strike-slip boundary involving the Indian and Eurasian plates. More than 2,000 people died.
tq: Use the fault type and plate pair to distinguish a recent earthquake event.

s: India forms part of which major seismic belt?
x: India lies in the Alpine-Himalayan seismic belt, which extends eastward through the North-East into Myanmar.
tq: Recall the major global seismic belt associated with India.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: The Indian Plate is moving approximately how far northward each year into the Eurasian Plate?
x: The Indian Plate moves northward into the Eurasian Plate at approximately 5 centimetres per year.
tq: Identify the central value in a set of plausible plate-motion rates.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: Which fault marks the Indian–Eurasian plate boundary in Myanmar?
x: In Myanmar, the Sagaing Fault marks the continuation of the Indian–Eurasian boundary through the eastern part of the seismic belt.
tq: Locate the named fault along the eastward continuation of the Himalayan seismic belt.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: Which of the following regions is NOT identified as a prone area for significant earthquake activity in India?
x: Kutch, the North-East and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are earthquake-prone areas. Visakhapatnam is cited as an example of a low-risk stable-shield area.
tq: Find the location that does not belong to the group of earthquake-prone regions.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Liquefaction is a particular concern in the Indo-Gangetic plain.
2. Peninsular faults associated with Latur and Koyna can produce earthquakes.
3. The Himalaya, North-East and Andaman and Nicobar Islands are among the earthquake-prone regions of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. Earthquake vulnerability in India is associated with Himalayan and North-Eastern regions, liquefaction-prone alluvial plains, peninsular faults and the Andaman and Nicobar region.
tq: Combine regional distribution with the associated hazard or geological setting.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: Under IS 1893:2016, which sequence correctly represents the seismic zones from lower to higher risk?
o: Zone II, Zone III, Zone IV, Zone V
Zone V, Zone IV, Zone III, Zone II
Zone III, Zone II, Zone V, Zone IV
Zone II, Zone IV, Zone III, Zone V
x: Under the four-zone map in force, Zone II represents low risk, Zone III moderate risk, Zone IV high risk and Zone V very high risk.
tq: Arrange the zones by increasing risk rather than by geographical location.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched under the seismic zoning classification in force?
x: Zone III is classified as a moderate-risk zone. Zone II is low, Zone IV is high and Zone V is very high risk.
tq: Check the exact risk label attached to each numerical zone.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: Which of the following areas is included in Zone V under the seismic zoning map in force?
x: Kutch is included in Zone V, the very-high-risk zone. Visakhapatnam and Hyderabad are examples of Zone II, while Vijayawada is cited under Zone III.
tq: Distinguish locations by their assigned seismic-risk zones.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: Delhi, the remaining Himalayan foothills and the Indo-Gangetic belt are generally placed in which seismic zone?
x: Delhi, the rest of the Himalayan foothills and the Indo-Gangetic belt are cited as examples of Zone IV, the high-risk zone.
tq: Associate a regional cluster with its common seismic zone.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: Which of the following cities is cited as an example of a Zone III location?
x: Vijayawada is cited as an example of Zone III, which represents moderate risk. Visakhapatnam and Hyderabad are examples of Zone II.
tq: Separate nearby Andhra locations by their stated seismic classification.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s:
With reference to Andhra Pradesh, consider the following statements:
1. Most of the state lies in Zones II and III.
2. Andhra Pradesh has no area in Zone V.
3. Andhra Pradesh is classified entirely as a very-high-risk state.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Most of Andhra Pradesh lies in Zones II and III, and it has no area in Zone V. It is not entirely a very-high-risk state, so statement 3 is false.
tq: Reject the extreme statement while retaining the two precise regional facts.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: Which of the following States or Union Territories has no area in Zone V?
x: Andhra Pradesh has no area in Zone V. Assam, Bihar and Jammu and Kashmir are identified as having areas in Zone V.
tq: Use the exception-based regional comparison to identify the outlier.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: Zone I was merged into which zone after the 1993 Latur earthquake?
x: After the 1993 Latur earthquake, Zone I was merged into Zone II, resulting in the four-zone classification under IS 1893:2002.
tq: Link a classification change to the event that prompted it.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Withdrawal of IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025
B. Notification of IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025
C. 1993 Latur earthquake
D. Bhuj earthquake
x: The correct order is the 1993 Latur earthquake, the 2001 Bhuj earthquake, notification of the 2025 revision on 6 November 2025, and its withdrawal on 3 March 2026.
tq: Use the first and last events, then place the two intermediate dates.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: The revised IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025 was notified by BIS on which date?
x: BIS notified the revised IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025 on 6 November 2025.
tq: Distinguish the notification date from the later withdrawal and review dates.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: Which feature was introduced by the IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025 revision?
o: The abolition of all seismic zones in India
The exclusion of the North-East from the highest-risk category
The restoration of Zone I as the lowest zone
A new top Zone VI covering parts of Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch
x: The 2025 revision introduced a new top Zone VI for parts of Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch, and placed more than 60% of India’s landmass in moderate-to-high zones.
tq: Identify the distinctive institutional change rather than a reversed zoning claim.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: The 2025 revision of IS 1893 was withdrawn on 3 March 2026 primarily after objections relating to which issue?
o: The inability to identify earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above
The absence of earthquake data from the North-East
The replacement of the National Seismological Network
The cost implications raised by MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA
x: The 2025 revision was withdrawn after MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA objected to the cost implications. The 2016 code was restored.
tq: Match the policy rollback with the specific administrative objection.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: Which code is currently restored after the withdrawal of the 2025 seismic zoning revision?
x: The withdrawal of the 2025 revision restored IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016 as the code in force.
tq: Distinguish the currently restored standard from the withdrawn revision.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the withdrawn 2025 seismic zoning map:
1. It was built by IIT-Madras for the NDMA.
2. It used a probabilistic seismic hazard assessment model.
3. It used 69,519 earthquake events and 36 seismogenic zones.
4. It set peak ground acceleration values from 0.15 g to 0.75 g across Zones II to VI.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All four statements are correct. The withdrawn map was prepared by IIT-Madras for NDMA using PSHA, 69,519 events, 36 seismogenic zones and PGA values of 0.15–0.75 g.
tq: Check each technical specification separately before selecting the coded combination.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: Which body is to receive the report of the review panel concerning the withdrawn seismic zoning revision?
x: The review panel is to submit its report to the Cabinet Secretariat.
tq: Identify the authority associated with the pending review process.
sec: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

s: The National Seismological Network of India consists of how many observatories?
x: The National Seismological Network operated by the National Centre for Seismology consists of 160 observatories.
tq: Distinguish the network size from the separate GNSS-station figure and event count.

s: The National Centre for Seismology detects which combination of earthquakes through its monitoring network?
o: Only earthquakes capable of producing tsunamis
Indian earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above and global earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 and above
Indian earthquakes of magnitude 1.0 and global earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above
Only earthquakes occurring in the Himalayan region
x: The network detects every Indian earthquake of magnitude 3.0 or above and global earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or above, including tsunami-capable events.
tq: Separate the two magnitude thresholds instead of treating them as identical.

s: The first seismological observatory in India was established at which place in 1898?
x: India’s first seismological observatory was established at Alipore in Calcutta in 1898.
tq: Recall the earliest observatory by combining its place and year.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: NCS — 34 GNSS stations for crustal strain
GSI — 34 GNSS stations for tracking crustal strain
NCS — first observatory at Alipore in 1898
x: The Geological Survey of India tracks crustal strain through 34 GNSS stations. The 160-observatory network is operated by the NCS.
tq: Avoid swapping the monitoring agencies and their respective functions.

s: RISEQ, the earthquake-related app of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, is now known by which name?
x: The MoES app RISEQ is now called “Bhookamp.” IndiaQuake is the public-alert app of the National Centre for Seismology.
tq: Discriminate between two similarly themed earthquake applications.

s: Which application provides public earthquake alerts through the National Centre for Seismology?
o: RISEQ only under its former name
x: The NCS’s IndiaQuake app provides public earthquake alerts. RISEQ, now called Bhookamp, is the MoES app referred to in the monitoring system.
tq: Use the app-function distinction rather than relying only on similar names.

s: India developed its Tsunami Early Warning System after which event?
x: India built its Tsunami Early Warning System after the 2004 Sumatra earthquake and tsunami.
tq: Match the warning-system initiative with the triggering disaster.

s:
With reference to seismic waves, consider the following statements:
1. S-waves are transverse waves.
2. S-waves can propagate through liquids.
3. The absence of S-waves beyond about 105° from the epicentre is evidence that the outer core is liquid.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: S-waves involve shear motion perpendicular to the direction of travel and propagate only through solids. Their absence beyond about 105° indicates the liquid nature of the outer core.
tq: Eliminate the statement that reverses the solid-only property of S-waves.
sec: Seismic waves - order, motion, damage  [other exams]

s: Love and Rayleigh waves are collectively classified as:
x: Love and Rayleigh waves move along the Earth's surface and are classified as surface waves.
tq: Test the exact classification of closely related seismic waves.
sec: Seismic waves - order, motion, damage  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the movement and damaging potential of surface waves?
o: They move through the outer core and cause limited damage.
They arrive last and generally cause the greatest damage.
They arrive first and produce compressional motion only.
They travel only through liquids and have no particle motion.
x: Surface waves arrive after the body waves and usually cause the greatest damage. Love waves show side-to-side motion, while Rayleigh waves have a rolling motion.
tq: Compare arrival time, motion and damage rather than memorising one feature alone.
sec: Seismic waves - order, motion, damage  [other exams]

s: At the Mohorovicic discontinuity, the speed of P-waves increases approximately from:
x: The speed of P-waves jumps from about 6.9 km/s to 8.1 km/s at the Moho, named after Mohorovicic.
tq: Identify the correct numerical range from the two values forming the discontinuity.
sec: Seismic waves - order, motion, damage  [other exams]

s:
Assertion (A): The outer core of the Earth is considered liquid.
Reason (R): S-waves do not pass beyond approximately 105° from the earthquake epicentre.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both statements are true. Since S-waves cannot travel through liquids, their absence beyond the shadow zone supports the conclusion that the outer core is liquid.
tq: Check whether the seismic observation directly explains the inference about the Earth's interior.
sec: Seismic waves - order, motion, damage  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following belts is associated with the greatest concentration of earthquakes in the world?
x: The Circum-Pacific belt, also called the Ring of Fire, contains the world's greatest concentration of earthquakes and is associated largely with subduction around the Pacific basin.
tq: Use the ranking of earthquake belts to select the most active belt.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Belt)
a. Pacific Ring of Fire
b. Mid-Atlantic belt
c. Mediterranean-Himalayan belt
 d. Hotspot belt

List-II (Plate setting or process)
i. Mantle plume beneath a moving plate
 ii. Divergent ridge
 iii. Subduction around a basin
 iv. Continental collision

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: The Pacific Ring of Fire is linked to subduction, the Mid-Atlantic belt to a divergent ridge, the Mediterranean-Himalayan belt to continental collision, and hotspots to mantle plumes.
tq: Start with the sure plate-setting pair and eliminate codes containing a wrong association.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: Chile lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire, not the Mid-Atlantic belt. Iceland is associated with the Mid-Atlantic belt, the Himalayas with the Alpine-Himalayan belt, and Hawaii with a hotspot.
tq: Find the location that belongs to a different seismic belt.

s: The earthquakes associated with mid-oceanic ridges are generally:
x: Mid-oceanic ridge earthquakes are generally shallow and milder, reflecting activity at divergent plate boundaries.
tq: Use the depth-and-severity comparison among the major earthquake belts.

s:
Which of the following 2026 earthquake events was reported with the correct magnitude and location?
1. Flores, Indonesia — magnitude 7.7
2. Colombia — magnitude 7.4
3. Kyushu, Japan — magnitude 7.1
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: The reported 2026 events included the magnitude 7.7 Flores earthquake, the magnitude 7.4 Colombia earthquake and the magnitude 7.1 Kyushu earthquake.
tq: Verify each location–magnitude pair independently before selecting the coded combination.

s: The 2026 earthquake in Colombia mentioned in the seismic-event record occurred on:
x: The Colombia earthquake of magnitude 7.4 was reported on 12 August 2026 and caused more than 100 deaths.
tq: Distinguish closely spaced dates by matching the event with its location.

s: Which combination of conditions is most conducive to the generation of a tsunami?
o: Magnitude below 5.0, deep focus and horizontal movement only
Magnitude above 6.5, shallow focus and vertical uplift of the sea floor
Volcanic ash fall without any displacement of water
Deep continental earthquake and subsidence of an inland basin
x: A tsunami generally requires an earthquake of magnitude greater than 6.5, a focus shallower than approximately 70 km and vertical uplift of the sea floor.
tq: Apply the necessary-condition test instead of relying on magnitude alone.

s: Approximately what proportion of tsunamis originate from megathrust earthquakes at subduction zones?
x: More than 80 percent of tsunamis originate from megathrust earthquakes occurring at subduction zones.
tq: Select the quantitative threshold associated with the dominant tsunami source.

s:
Match the earthquake effect with the region or cause most closely associated with it:

List-I (Effect)
a. Landslides
b. Liquefaction
c. Seismic seiches
 d. Fires

List-II (Associated setting or cause)
i. Broken gas and power lines
 ii. Lakes and reservoirs
 iii. Fragile Himalaya and North-East
 iv. Soft soils of the Indo-Gangetic Plain

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Earthquakes trigger landslides in the fragile Himalaya and North-East, liquefaction in soft Indo-Gangetic soils, seiches in lakes and reservoirs, and fires through broken gas and power lines.
tq: Match each hazard with its distinctive physical setting or immediate cause.

s: Narcondam, located in the Andaman Sea, is associated with which of the following?
o: An extinct volcanic hill and the Asiatic lion
A dormant volcano and the Narcondam hornbill
India's only active volcano and the Nicobar pigeon
A flood-basalt plateau and the Great Indian bustard
x: Narcondam is a dormant volcano in the Andaman Sea and is the home of the Narcondam hornbill.
tq: Combine location, volcanic status and associated species to resolve a confusable pair.
sec: Volcanoes in India - active vs dormant, Deccan Traps origin  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Deccan Traps?
o: Fissure-related flood-basalt outpourings on the Maharashtra Plateau near the end of the Cretaceous
An intrusive granite batholith formed in Ladakh during the Cenozoic Era
A chain of dormant volcanic cones formed in the Andaman Sea during the Quaternary period
A group of extinct volcanic hills confined to Kutch
x: The Deccan Traps are fissure or flood-basalt outpourings on the Maharashtra Plateau that occurred at the end of the Cretaceous and are linked to the Reunion hotspot.
tq: Use origin, location and geological age together rather than a single keyword.
sec: Volcanoes in India - active vs dormant, Deccan Traps origin  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The Deccan Traps are linked in origin with the:
x: The Deccan Traps are linked to activity of the Reunion hotspot near the end of the Cretaceous.
tq: Discriminate among similarly named hotspot examples using the associated landform.
sec: Volcanoes in India - active vs dormant, Deccan Traps origin  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: A mud volcano at Diglipur is distinguished from a lava volcano because it ejects:
x: The Diglipur mud volcano ejects mud, water and methane rather than lava. Its activity is driven by tectonic pressure on the active Andaman Arc subduction zone.
tq: Distinguish a process by its actual ejecta rather than by the word volcano.
sec: Volcanoes in India - active vs dormant, Deccan Traps origin  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Lopolith — wavy mass in a folded structure
Phacolith — wavy mass at the base of a syncline or top of an anticline
Laccolith — vertical wall cutting across rock beds
x: A phacolith is a wavy intrusive mass occurring at the base of a syncline or the top of an anticline. A lopolith is saucer-shaped, a laccolith is dome-shaped with a flat base, and a dyke is a vertical wall.
tq: Match each intrusive form with its distinctive shape or structural position.
sec: Volcanic landforms - intrusive and extrusive  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which intrusive volcanic body is a huge dome of granite cooled deep within the crust and commonly forms the core of mountains?
x: A batholith is a huge dome-like mass of granite that cools deep in the crust and may form the core of a mountain range.
tq: Identify the landform from its scale, composition and depth of emplacement.
sec: Volcanic landforms - intrusive and extrusive  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
Consider the following statements about intrusive volcanic forms:
1. A laccolith is dome-shaped and has a flat base.
2. A lopolith is saucer-shaped.
3. A sill is a horizontal sheet parallel to the rock beds.
4. A dyke is a vertical wall cutting across the beds.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All four statements are correct. These forms are distinguished mainly by their shape and their relation to the surrounding rock beds.
tq: Check each form against its geometric description and relation to bedding.
sec: Volcanic landforms - intrusive and extrusive  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The Deccan Traps were fed by which type of intrusive structure cutting across the rock beds?
x: Dykes are vertical walls that cut across rock beds and fed the fissure eruptions associated with the Deccan Traps in western Maharashtra.
tq: Connect the structural form of an intrusion with its role in feeding surface lava.
sec: Volcanic landforms - intrusive and extrusive  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The Ladakh Magmatic Arc lies between which two suture zones?
o: Main Boundary and Main Central suture zones
x: The Ladakh Magmatic Arc is located in the Trans-Himalaya between the Indus and Shyok suture zones.
tq: Use the paired geographical boundaries to identify the magmatic arc.
sec: Volcanic landforms - intrusive and extrusive  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the geological development of the Ladakh Magmatic Arc?
o: It formed when the Neo-Tethys plate subducted under Eurasia and underwent a batholith phase from about 160 Ma to less than 45 Ma.
It formed from the Reunion hotspot during the end of the Cretaceous and consists only of flood basalts.
It formed at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge through present-day divergent movement.
It developed when the Indian plate subducted beneath the Pacific plate during the Quaternary period.
x: The Ladakh Magmatic Arc formed through subduction of the Neo-Tethys plate beneath Eurasia and experienced a batholith phase from approximately 160 Ma to less than 45 Ma.
tq: Combine the tectonic process with the geological time interval and reject unrelated settings.
sec: Volcanic landforms - intrusive and extrusive  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following is an extrusive volcanic landform?
x: Lava plateaus, cinder and composite cones, craters, calderas and lava flows are extrusive volcanic landforms. Batholiths, lopoliths and phacoliths are intrusive forms.
tq: Separate surface-formed extrusive features from underground intrusive bodies.
sec: Volcanic landforms - intrusive and extrusive  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Etna is located in which of the following regions and is characterised by which status?
x: Etna is an active stratovolcano located in Sicily, Italy.
tq: Use the country-region and volcano-status pair together to avoid confusing Etna with other Italian volcanoes.

s: Which one of the following statements regarding Mount Etna is correct?
o: It is Europe's largest and most active volcano, rises to about 3,300 m and became a UNESCO site in 2013.
It is Africa's highest peak and has been dormant since 1707.
It is the world's highest active volcano at 6,893 m.
It is an extinct volcano that buried Pompeii in AD 79.
x: Etna is Europe's largest and most active volcano, is approximately 3,300 m high and has been a UNESCO site since 2013.
tq: Distinguish closely related volcano facts by checking the continent, height, status and historical association.

s: The volcano associated with the burial of Pompeii in AD 79 is:
x: Mount Vesuvius is an active volcano in Italy and buried Pompeii in AD 79.
tq: Apply the famous-event association to identify the correct volcano.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: Ojos del Salado is in Chile and is the world's highest active volcano, at 6,893 m; it is not dormant.
tq: Find the mismatched status by separating country facts from active-dormant classifications.

s: The last recorded eruption of Fujiyama mentioned in the geographical record was in:
x: Fujiyama in Japan is dormant, and its last eruption occurred in 1707.
tq: Test the precise historical year rather than relying only on the volcano's country or status.

s: Which volcano is recognised as the world's highest active volcano?
x: Ojos del Salado in Chile is the world's highest active volcano, with an elevation of 6,893 m.
tq: Use the superlative and the numerical height as the decisive clues.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Volcan de Fuego is Guatemala's most active stratovolcano.
2. Its Strombolian eruptions may occur every 15–20 minutes.
3. It erupted again in June 2026.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct: Volcan de Fuego is Guatemala's most active stratovolcano, has frequent Strombolian eruptions and erupted again in June 2026.
tq: Check the location, eruption frequency and recent-event details independently before selecting the coded combination.

s: Popocatepetl, which has been active since 1994, is located in:
x: Popocatepetl is an active volcano in Mexico and has been active since 1994.
tq: Use the country-status-year combination to distinguish neighbouring Latin American volcanoes.

s: Which of the following recent volcano-related events is correctly matched?
x: Mayon is in the Philippines and is noted for its symmetrical composite-cone form. Mount Dukono is in Halmahera, Indonesia, while Mount Spurr is in Alaska's Aleutian Arc.
tq: Match each volcano with its location and distinguishing description, rejecting swapped-location traps.

s: Which of the following is NOT a volcanic product?
x: Pyroclastic debris, volcanic bombs and lava are volcanic products. Atmospheric air is not listed as a volcanic product.
tq: Classify the physical materials emitted or produced by volcanoes and identify the outsider.

s: Which gas is present in the greatest proportion among the principal gases released by volcanoes?
x: Volcanic gases consist mostly of water vapour, followed by carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide.
tq: Recall the stated order of abundance rather than confusing gases with solid volcanic products.

s: A volcano that is presently quiet but may erupt in the future is classified as:
x: A dormant volcano is quiet at present but retains the possibility of erupting. An extinct volcano is not expected to erupt.
tq: Discriminate between the similar status terms dormant and extinct by focusing on future eruptive possibility.

s: A volcano is considered extinct when:
o: It is quiet temporarily but may erupt
It is erupting or has erupted recently
x: An extinct volcano is one from which no eruption is expected; temporary quietness describes a dormant volcano.
tq: Compare the status definitions directly and reject the tempting reversal of dormant and extinct.

s: Which one of the following volcanoes is an example of a shield volcano?
x: Mauna Loa is a shield volcano formed by fluid basaltic lava and characterised by gentle slopes.
tq: Link the volcano example to the defining lava type and slope profile.

s: Shield volcanoes are generally characterised by:
o: Several vents and overlapping lava domes in every case
Fluid basaltic lava and gentle slopes
A large depression formed only by erosion
Thick viscous lava, steep cones and explosive eruptions
x: Shield volcanoes have fluid basaltic lava and gentle slopes. Thick viscous lava and explosive steep cones are characteristic of composite volcanoes.
tq: Use the contrast between lava viscosity and slope to distinguish shield and composite volcanoes.

s:
Consider the following statements about composite or stratovolcanoes:
1. They generally have thick and viscous lava.
2. They commonly form steep cones.
3. They are associated with explosive eruptions.
4. They constitute approximately 60% of the Earth's volcanoes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All four statements are correct. Composite or stratovolcanoes have viscous lava, steep cones, explosive activity and constitute approximately 60% of Earth's volcanoes.
tq: Test a group of defining characteristics together, including the quantitative share.

s: A large depression formed by the collapse of a volcano after an explosive eruption is called a:
x: A caldera is a large depression produced by collapse following an explosive eruption.
tq: Identify the landform from its formation process rather than from an example alone.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Mauna Loa — caldera formed by explosive collapse
Mount Aso — one of the world's largest calderas
Etna — complex volcano with several overlapping vents only
Dukono — shield volcano with gentle basaltic slopes
x: Mount Aso is one of the world's largest calderas. Mauna Loa is a shield volcano, while Dukono is listed as a complex volcano.
tq: Start with the distinctive example of a landform and then eliminate type-example reversals.

s: Complex or compound volcanoes are distinguished by the presence of:
o: Several vents, overlapping cones and lava domes
Only fluid basaltic lava and very gentle slopes
A single crater with no secondary vents
No lava and no eruptive products
x: Complex or compound volcanoes contain several vents, overlapping cones and lava domes. Taal and Dukono are examples.
tq: Recall the structural features of the volcano type before considering its examples.

s: Which of the following is correctly matched with a complex or compound volcano?
x: Taal in the Philippines is a complex or compound volcano. Dukono is in Indonesia, while Mount Aso is a caldera in Japan.
tq: Use the sure example-location pair and reject nearby country substitutions.

s: Which statement correctly distinguishes Strombolian and Vulcanian eruptions?
o: Vulcanian eruptions consist only of gentle lava flows.
Strombolian eruptions are frequent and mild, whereas Vulcanian eruptions are more explosive.
Strombolian eruptions are always more explosive than Vulcanian eruptions.
Both terms refer exclusively to dormant volcanoes.
x: Strombolian eruptions involve frequent, mild bursts of bombs and ash, whereas Vulcanian eruptions are more explosive.
tq: Compare the intensity and nature of the two similarly named eruption styles.

s: A seismic doublet refers to:
o: Two aftershocks of exactly equal magnitude from the same rupture
Two independent earthquakes of similar size
Two volcanic eruptions from adjacent craters
One earthquake followed by a tsunami
x: A seismic doublet consists of two independent earthquakes of similar size. Such an event was described near Caracas on the Caribbean–South American strike-slip boundary.
tq: Resolve the technical term by separating independent similar events from aftershocks or related hazards.

s: The Caracas seismic doublet occurred on which type of plate boundary?
x: The Caracas doublet occurred on the Caribbean–South American strike-slip boundary.
tq: Associate the event with its named boundary type and avoid substituting a generic plate-boundary category.

s: Which of the following recent earthquake-event pairs is correctly matched?
o: M 7.7 — off Flores Island, Indonesia — August 2026
x: An M 7.7 earthquake struck off Flores Island, Indonesia, on 18 August 2026. The other events have been paired with incorrect locations or magnitudes.
tq: Check magnitude, location and date together to defeat swapped-event distractors.

s: The M 8.8 megathrust earthquake off Kamchatka in August 2025 was notable because it:
o: Produced a tsunami that completely inundated the Pacific coast
Occurred on the Caracas strike-slip boundary
x: Despite its M 8.8 megathrust magnitude, the Kamchatka earthquake caused only a limited tsunami.
tq: Focus on the unusual consequence of the event rather than inferring impact solely from magnitude.

s:
Consider the following statements about seismicity in Andhra Pradesh:
1. Most of Andhra Pradesh lies in Seismic Zones II and III.
2. Reservoir-triggered tremors cannot be ruled out near Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam and Polavaram.
3. Old faults in the Eastern Ghats are relevant to the possibility of tremors.
4. Visakhapatnam lies in Zone V.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Visakhapatnam is in Zone II, not Zone V.
tq: Find the location-based false statement by checking the specific seismic zone assigned to Visakhapatnam.

s: An earthquake of magnitude 4.4, at a depth of 5 km, near Koraput–Jeypore shook which areas in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Araku and Paderu in ASR district
x: The M 4.4 earthquake near Koraput–Jeypore in Odisha, at a depth of 5 km, shook Araku and Paderu in the ASR district.
tq: Combine the magnitude, depth and affected-location clues to identify the event precisely.

s: The withdrawn earthquake hazard map was based on how many earthquake events and seismogenic zones?
x: The withdrawn map was based on 69,519 events and 36 seismogenic zones.
tq: Keep the two numerical components paired; the distractors reverse or alter one of the figures.

s: Which statement correctly describes the change concerning Zone VI in IS 1893:2025?
o: Zone VI was notified and subsequently withdrawn on 3 March 2026.
Zone VI was notified permanently on 3 March 2026.
Zone VI was withdrawn before being notified in 2025.
Zone VI was notified only for Andhra Pradesh and retained without change.
x: Zone VI was notified in IS 1893:2025 and was subsequently withdrawn on 3 March 2026.
tq: Track the sequence of notification followed by withdrawal and reject reversed timelines.

s: Experts criticised the restored 2016 earthquake-hazard values mainly because they considered them:
o: Applicable only to coastal Andhra Pradesh
x: Experts argued that the restored 2016 hazard values were too low for the Himalaya. NDMA, in contrast, described the new values as too high.
tq: Separate the contrasting positions of experts and NDMA instead of treating both criticisms as identical.

s: Which of the following statements about earthquake safety and construction is correct?
o: Construction cost is irrelevant to the debate over PSHA-based codes.
Approximately 95% of earthquake deaths occur in poorly built one- to three-storey houses.
Retrofitting is unnecessary when a building follows no seismic code.
Earthquake deaths occur almost exclusively in high-rise steel buildings.
x: About 95% of earthquake deaths occur in poorly built one- to three-storey houses. The debate also involves balancing safer PSHA-based codes against construction costs.
tq: Apply the risk statistic to a built-environment scenario and reject exaggerated building claims.

s: Which of the following is the FIRST step among NDMA's six pillars of seismic safety?
o: Replacing all reservoirs with underground water tanks
Building according to IS 1893, IS 4326 and IS 13920, along with prioritising important buildings for retrofitting
Banning all construction in Seismic Zone II
x: The first pillar begins with construction according to IS 1893, IS 4326 and IS 13920, together with retrofitting priority buildings.
tq: Identify the institutional safety measure that directly addresses structural vulnerability.

s: Which one of the following statements about Andhra Pradesh and earthquake risk is correct?
o: Andhra Pradesh lies entirely in Zone V and has no reservoir-related seismic risk.
The Eastern Ghats have no old faults relevant to seismicity.
Only coastal areas of Andhra Pradesh can experience earthquakes.
Although Andhra Pradesh lies mainly in Zones II and III, reservoir-triggered tremors remain possible near major reservoirs and along old Eastern Ghats faults.
x: Andhra Pradesh is mainly in Zones II and III, but tremors associated with reservoirs and old Eastern Ghats faults cannot be ruled out.
tq: Combine the general regional classification with the important stated exception.
